clinicalPearls: Torsion is a gynaecological emergency in which the ovary, often with the fallopian tube, twists on its pedicle and compromises its blood supply, threatening ovarian viability
It classically presents with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, often colicky and associated with nausea and vomiting, sometimes provoked by exertion or a change in position
An enlarged ovary or an ovarian mass, particularly cysts around five centimetres or larger, predisposes to torsion, so it is uncommon in a normal-sized ovary
Doppler ultrasound may show reduced or absent flow, but preserved arterial flow does not exclude torsion because dual blood supply and intermittent twisting can maintain signals
Torsion can occur in pregnancy, especially after ovulation induction with enlarged ovaries, and in premenarchal girls in whom the diagnosis is easily missed
Prompt surgical intervention, usually laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary, is preferred over oophorectomy even when the ovary looks dusky, as tissue often recovers
The classic error is delay: repeated observation while awaiting imaging or normalisation of pain risks irreversible ischaemic loss of the ovary
Intermittent torsion produces recurrent self-limiting episodes of pain and warrants evaluation before a definitive infarction occurs
reference.pathophysiology: When the ovary or adnexa rotates about the infundibulopelvic and utero-ovarian ligaments, the lower-pressure venous and lymphatic drainage is occluded first, producing congestion and marked ovarian oedema and enlargement. Continued or tightening rotation eventually compromises arterial inflow, leading to ischaemia, haemorrhagic infarction, and necrosis. Because arterial flow may persist longer than venous outflow owing to the thicker arterial wall and dual blood supply, viability can be maintained for a variable period, defining a window in which detorsion can salvage the ovary.
additionalDifferentials: Pelvic inflammatory disease or tubo-ovarian abscess
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal or transabdominal pelvic ultrasound with Doppler to assess ovarian size, mass, and blood flow
Urine or serum beta-hCG to exclude pregnancy and ectopic
Full blood count and inflammatory markers to help exclude infective or appendiceal causes
Diagnostic laparoscopy, which is both confirmatory and therapeutic when suspicion is high
Pelvic MRI in selected non-acute or pregnant cases when ultrasound is inconclusive
redFlags: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with an adnexal mass, mandating urgent assessment to preserve the ovary
Persistent pain with peritonism suggesting ischaemia or necrosis
Haemodynamic instability raising concern for haemorrhage or a ruptured ectopic
Signs of sepsis suggesting necrotic or infected adnexa
Recurrent episodic pain indicating intermittent torsion needing prompt surgical evaluation
reference.prognosis: When detorsion is performed promptly the ovary usually recovers function even if it appeared ischaemic at surgery, and future fertility is generally preserved. Delayed diagnosis leads to infarction requiring oophorectomy and loss of that ovary's function; recurrence can occur, and oophoropexy may be considered in selected cases such as recurrent torsion or a normal ovary in a child.
pitfalls: Excluding torsion because Doppler shows preserved arterial flow
Delaying surgery for repeated imaging or observation while ischaemia progresses
Performing oophorectomy on a dusky ovary that would recover after simple detorsion
Failing to consider torsion in premenarchal girls and pregnant women
Missing intermittent torsion by attributing recurrent pain to functional cysts
management: Perform emergency laparoscopic detorsion to restore blood flow, conserving the ovary even when it appears dusky since the tissue commonly recovers
Remove a causative ovarian cyst or mass by cystectomy at the same operation to treat the predisposing lesion
Reserve oophorectomy for a frankly necrotic, non-viable ovary
Consider oophoropexy to fix the ovary where torsion is recurrent or the pedicle is abnormally long
Give preoperative analgesia and antiemetics and keep the patient nil by mouth in preparation for urgent theatre
Do not exclude the diagnosis on preserved Doppler arterial flow; proceed to prompt diagnostic laparoscopy when clinical suspicion is high, as delay leads to infarction
Involve gynaecology urgently, with counselling on ovarian conservation and future fertility
